newsitem.title: USA: NATO mulling action against Bosnia war criminals.
newsitem.headline: NATO mulling action against Bosnia war criminals.

text.p: The United States and Europe are considering action against suspected war criminals in Bosnia but no decision has been made, U.S. officials said on Friday.
One key idea being discussed was creation of a special police force to arrest indicted war criminals. However other options were also under discussion, the officials said.

Some officials told Reuters they suspected the planning was much farther along than other senior officials would admit. But there was concern that premature disclosure of details could prompt suspects indicted by the international War Crimes Tribunal in the Hague to flee, officials said.

Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum, the special envoy on Bosnia, told reporters at the Overseas Writers luncheon that: "There is a judgment by everybody that some kind of international action is useful."
But "there is at the moment no consensus on any kind of special police or military or any other unit."

"We are thinking both internally and are talking with our allies ... about a more integrated comprehensive approach to the war criminal question. We're not satisfied with our experience during the past year in apprehending war criminals," he said.

Most of those indicted by the war crimes tribunal remained at large more than one year after the Bosnia peace agreement was signed in 1995. The two most prominent suspects, wartime Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and retired Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, continued to exert influence in Bosnia's serb republic.
The idea of the special police force was first proposed publicly by U.S. General John Shalikashvili, chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, last month.

He said the mandate for NATO's new 18-month peacekeeping mission in Bosnia -- successor to the IFOR implementation force -- did not call for its troops to arrest war crimes suspects. But a separate police force should be formed to go after indicted war criminals who have not been handed over as required by the Dayton peace accords, he said.

Kornblum said on Friday, however, that "it's not just so simple to say we're going to go out and get a bunch of soldiers to find them... In the first place, exactly pinpointing them so that you can do a military operation ... is not that easy."

Some European allies were lukewarm to the special police unit idea. Countries like France and Italy, with the paramilitary capabilities to perform such tasks, reportedly worried such a mission could involve dangerous firefights and subject their forces to reprisals from belligerents loyal to the war crimes suspects.

U.S. officials denied European concerns had put the special police unit idea on hold. "It's not that the Europeans have been negative about it. It's just that there's a lot of complicated questions" associated with the proposal, one official told Reuters.

Officials said that now that U.S.-led peace efforts in Bosnia have ended the fighting and begun to make progress in rebuilding the country politically and economically, the United States and its allies have made bringing war criminals to justice a major priority.
